blocks.text: Chapter 7.
Superteams: When Groups Beat Their Best Member
Seventh night, friend — and it begins with a map nobody checked.

April 1961. President Kennedy's advisers — the most credentialed team ever assembled in Washington — approve a CIA plan: land 1,400 Cuban exiles at the Bay of Pigs and topple Castro. The invasion collapses in days, the exiles pinned on the beach and captured. And here is the detail that should haunt every meeting room on earth: the fallback plan said a failed force could melt into the mountains — across eighty miles of impassable swamp that lay between the beach and those mountains. A glance at a map would have killed the plan. Around that polished table, nobody looked.
The same men, twice

Psychologist Irving Janis named the disease groupthink — you met it in Duke's fire, friend, and here is its origin story: in cohesive groups, harmony feels good and dissent feels like betrayal, so members self-censor, read silence as agreement, and converge without testing anything. Not stupidity — the best and brightest did this. A predictable byproduct of small groups whenever nothing in the process forces disagreement into the open.

So should you forecast alone? Not so fast — remember Galton's ox: aggregation pools scraps of information no single mind holds. Echo chamber versus information pool — which force wins? The most stunning evidence that the answer is process, not people comes from Kennedy himself.

Pause and guess: Eighteen months after the Bay of Pigs, largely THE SAME advisers faced the Cuban Missile Crisis — thirteen days on the edge of nuclear war. They performed brilliantly: a blockade, a negotiated missile withdrawal, catastrophe averted. What had changed?
Ready? Here is what happened.

The process — nothing else. After the fiasco, Kennedy ordered an inquiry into his own decision-making and rebuilt it to institutionalize skepticism: advisers were ordered to act as skeptical generalists — questioning everything, defending no turf; agenda and rank were suspended; the group split into subgroups that built rival options and cross-examined each other; and — the masterstroke — Kennedy periodically left the room, because he knew his presence bent people toward what they thought he wanted to hear. Same brains that blessed the swamp plan; excellent collective judgment once dissent became mandatory instead of costly. The lesson is exact, friend: groups don't have fixed IQs — they have designs, and designs can be fixed. Intel's Andy Grove found the same law in industry with "constructive confrontation" — unsparing debate aimed at ideas, never people, where challenging the boss is an obligation. Both words carry weight: confrontation without constructiveness is ego war; constructiveness without confrontation drifts back into polite groupthink.
The 23% experiment

Tetlock, true to form, refused to philosophize and ran the trial. Year two of the tournament: forecasters randomly assigned to work alone... or in online teams that could share, argue, and see each other's numbers. If groupthink dominated, teams should sink.

They soared: teams were 23% more accurate than individuals. The project had stacked the deck against groupthink with light-touch design — a primer on group pitfalls, explicit encouragement to treat disagreement as a resource — and one tool worth stealing tonight: precision questioning. Instead of the head-on "I disagree" (which triggers identity defense), drill into components: "What exactly do you mean by 'unlikely'? What's the evidence behind that piece? How does this step follow?" Assumptions surface; nobody bleeds.

Then the stronger test: superforecasters grouped into superteams of about a dozen. They dominated everything — crushing ordinary teams, and beating prediction markets (the mechanism economists expected to be unbeatable) by 15-30%. And instead of regressing, superforecasters kept improving inside teams. The friction was real — every team threatened to become too polite (rubber-stamping numbers to preserve warmth) or too abrasive (driving members out) — and the best navigated between, running collective postmortems on shared failures instead of assigning blame.
The givers

Why did these teams work when committees everywhere fail? Wharton's Adam Grant supplies a beautiful piece: his research sorts people into givers (contribute more than they extract), takers (the reverse), and matchers (tit for tat) — and finds givers at both extremes of performance: exploited givers sink, but strategic givers rise to the very top, because generosity compounds across a network.

Superteams ran on giver fuel: members spent hours hunting research and sharing it with teammates who might never reciprocate. In a competitive frame, that's arming your rivals; in a team scored on collective accuracy, it's exactly rational — one member's legwork lifts every forecast, and the generosity proved contagious. But sharing carries a hidden poison, friend: correlation. If everyone reads the same teammate's analysis, forecasts stop being independent draws — and the crowd's error-cancelling magic weakens. The best teams countered with active open-mindedness at the group level: treating each other's views as hypotheses, keeping dissenters engaged, and standing by the most useful question in teamwork: "what am I missing?"
Diversity trumps ability — and the winning algorithm

Now the counterintuitive mathematics of who belongs on the team. Economist Scott Page proved the diversity-trumps-ability result: under broad conditions, a group of diverse problem-solvers outperforms a group composed of clones of the single best one.
Pause and guess: How can a team of weaker-but-different thinkers beat a team of copies of the strongest thinker?
Ready? Here is what happened.

Because clones share the same blind spots — their errors are correlated, all falling in the same direction, and nothing cancels. Diverse thinkers err in different directions, and the errors annihilate each other while the shared signal accumulates — Galton's ox, engineered on purpose. (Ability still matters — you want skilled and different — but adding a new perspective can beat adding another copy of the star.) The superteams embodied it: retired programmers, pharmacists, film directors, social scientists, all attacking one question from different angles. And the tournament's final twist pushed the logic one step further: GJP's winning method — the one that beat every rival, including prediction markets and reportedly the classified-briefed analysts — pooled thousands of forecasts, weighted the better and fresher ones... and then extremized the aggregate: pushed a pooled 70% toward 85, away from 50. Why? Each forecaster holds only a fragment of the available information; if one person held every fragment, they'd be more confident than any individual actually is. Averaging bakes in the timidity of dispersed knowledge — extremizing simulates the fully-informed forecaster. One caveat worthy of the whole book: it works only when knowledge is genuinely dispersed — a tight team that has already pooled everything is already extremized, and pushing further adds error. Every tool works only when you know why it works.
Before you go

So: the swamp nobody mapped; the same men brilliant eighteen months later under a redesigned process; teams beating soloists by 23% and superteams beating markets; givers lifting everyone while diversity cancels what clones compound; and the algorithm that won it all by restoring the confidence dispersed knowledge steals. The arc is one idea at three scales, friend: a mind aggregates perspectives, a team aggregates minds, an algorithm aggregates teams — and at every level the winning move is identical: combine diverse, independent judgments, and let no single voice — including your own — drown out the rest.

One night remains. And it belongs to the hardest questions of all: do these methods survive contact with real power — leaders who must decide, not just predict? What did a Prussian field marshal know about balancing deliberation with decisiveness? And what of the black swan — Taleb's objection that the only events that truly matter are precisely the ones no tournament question can capture? Tomorrow, the finale: the humility that isn't meekness — and what foresight is actually for.
Key takeaways
Groupthink blessed the Bay of Pigs; the same advisers excelled in the Missile Crisis — groups have designs, not IQs, and designs can be fixed.
JFK's redesign: skeptical generalists, rank suspended, rival subgroups, and the leader leaving the room.
The randomized trial: teams beat individuals by 23%; superteams beat prediction markets by 15-30% and kept improving.
Precision questioning replaces "I disagree": drill into terms, evidence, and inference — assumptions surface without blood.
Givers power superteams, but guard independence: shared analysis breeds correlated error — keep asking "what am I missing?"
Diversity trumps cloned ability (different errors cancel), and extremized aggregation wins — but only when knowledge is truly dispersed.
